body:
Did you start work on this after our meeting last Thursday? Because damn, that would be fast.

Will try to properly review this in a couple of days, I had a brilliant (and fun to implement) idea for a massive optimization for the castle demo scene and got totally sidetracked.

Some things I noticed at a glance:
1. there is no emissive buffer right now, that is something that really needs to be added imo.
2. you could add a R8_UINT id buffer so that users can switch between different light shaders (that way people could still write their own light shader, their code would simply be inserted into a compute shader instead of the fragment shader). The same system could also be reused to add support for the different material types (SSS, aniso, rim, clearcoat) that you currently don't support.

> Did you start work on this after our meeting last Thursday? Because damn, that would be fast.

Yup, but I've had the idea for like forever..

> 1. there is no emissive buffer right now, that is something that really needs to be added imo.

No, not needed, ambient and emission is written directly into the final colour buffer. There is no need for further processing on these values for each light.

> 2. you could add a R8_UINT id buffer so that users can switch between different light shaders (that way people could still write their own light shader, their code would simply be inserted into a compute shader instead of the fragment shader). The same system could also be reused to add support for the different material types (SSS, aniso, rim, clearcoat) that you currently don't support.

This wouldn't work unless we'd run the computer shader for every shader or create one massive else if block with all the different light shaders.

I was thinking about writing the instance id into an R32_UINT buffer as we also need access to the layer masks (which I'm currently ignoring). But I'm worried that we already have 5 fullres buffers, at some point the sheer bandwidth usage is going to negate any performance deferred rendering could offer (My test project is already running slower with just the directional light than with forward+ as is, though I'm running on a 4080 and most of the performance is lost on updating shadowmaps).

> No, not needed, ambient and emission is written directly into the final colour buffer.

Oh yes, looks like I missed the ifdef unshaded when I was looking at this on my phone.

> This wouldn't work unless we'd run the computer shader for every shader or create one massive else if block with all the different light shaders.

Ok, crazy idea but hear me out. What if we turn the compute shader into a full screen triangle fragment shader? Then we could use compare op equal on the id buffer to let the early depth check determine when we actually need to run.
Alternatively we could try a two pass approach using compute shaders. Pass one creates pixel lists for each type of light shader that was used and pass two actually runs the shaders over these lists.

> My test project is already running slower with just the directional light than with forward+ as is

Yeah, that is why I was so hesitant in the meeting last week when it came to deferred. The early depth pass in combination with compare op equal already does a really good job at reducing overdraw to 0 and keeping texture read/writes as low as possible.
Any gains from deferred would have to come either from lower register pressure, better cache usage or us eliminating the depth prepass and thus saving vertex performance (But keep in mind that without the prepass we would have to fill the gbuffer even for fragments that will immediately be overwritten -> tons of unnecessary texture read & writes).

> Ok, crazy idea but hear me out. What if we turn the compute shader into a full screen triangle fragment shader? Then we could use compare op equal on the id buffer to let the early depth check determine when we actually need to run. Alternatively we could try a two pass approach using compute shaders. Pass one creates pixel lists for each type of light shader that was used and pass two actually runs the shaders over these lists.

I think we have unexplored options for optimisation when using a compute shader that we may miss out on when using fragment shaders. That said, I think any sort of duplication or branching to run different light shaders, is going to kill performance. Remember, the light shader is set per material, not per light, so you get a shader variant * lights situation.

Also we can't do the fragment output => light shader input bit because they are now disjoint (unless we want to write a sh*tton of data to buffers completely removing any hope of performance gains).
 
> > My test project is already running slower with just the directional light than with forward+ as is
> 
> Yeah, that is why I was so hesitant in the meeting last week when it came to deferred.

This really is the main reason why I wanted to do this for a long time. The thing is, on **modern** hardware the clustered Forward+ approach **is** faster than deferred rendering.

Deferred rendering is great on lower end hardware that can't make use of clustering, rendering on lower resolutions, with simpler lighting models.
But the reality is that where we want this, is mostly mobile. And with TBDR GPUs, they suffer greatly from the increased bandwidth usage of G-buffers, which increases exponentially when you increase resolution.

It will be interesting to see if we can optimise this to actually be faster on certain classes of GPUs, and have some really good metrics around this. We're definitely nowhere near knowing whether we won't get the desired performance or whether with rewriting the shaders to be further way from how the normal Forward+ renderer works, we have a winner. Its very possible we'd need much more structural changes (I still believe part of the problem is that we're working with far too much data just so we can support all the fancy stuff, ripping that all out might yield results).

But its also very likely that we find out for what Godot users expect as the graphics bar, on the hardware currently most prevalent, deferred rendering is a dead end. But people won't believe that until it's proven, especially because 5 years ago it was the beez kneez.
